notes: Three university-level documents (OIT AI guidelines, syllabus-statement page, teaching-center page); no school or computing policy found, course layer deferred. Units were aligned by source sentence, and the coders matched almost everywhere; most of the difference is that A split more sentences into units (A found 88 units, B 71). All 19 A-only and 2 B-only units were checked against the source and kept as real statements (facts and disclaimers in the IT guidelines, labour-market and benefit rationale in the teaching-center page); no unit was dropped. Main disagreements: (1) document stance of the IT guidelines, A permit vs B delegates, resolved to permit because the page welcomes AI with conditions and names no instructor decision; (2) unit_stance, where A often wrote require or restrict for verification and data-protection duties and B wrote neutral or encourage; resolved toward neutral when the unit is a duty or advice that neither bans nor allows AI use (not scored in the shares); (3) actor, student vs all for sentences addressed to 'users', resolved to all; (4) phase, general vs during-work for security cautions and for the sample ban statements, settled by what the sentence is about; (5) modality, must vs should and must-not vs should-not for 'please' and 'is crucial' wording, resolved to the softer should forms; (6) policy_type on borderline units: P09 vs P66 (communicating allowed uses, to P66), P09 vs P04 (specific instructions per assignment, to P04), P01 vs P22 (all-assessments ban, to P01), P20 vs P21 (own work sent to an LLM, to P20), P14 vs P12 and P14 vs P15 (AI feedback and role-play, to P14). The reconciler split one A unit that merged two rules (diligence and human oversight) into two units, one matched and one B-only. Shares are over matched units; stance over documents.
